n_intro: Everybody remembers where they were the day the world ended. I remember the day before. It was the best day I ever had, in Lone Keem, Maine.
n_wake: I was thirteen. The fog came in off the harbor every morning like it was checking on us. That Saturday, nothing in the world was wrong yet.
n_kitchen: My father could fix any engine in the county, but he could not make a pancake to save his life. My mother came home from her night shift smelling of hospital soap. We laughed a lot in that kitchen.
n_yard: Theo Lindqvist lived next door. He knew every horror movie ever made. Turns out, that does not help you one bit.
n_walt: Walt Abernathy was seventy four, and he still grew tomatoes too late in the year. He gave me his old compass that morning. I have it still.
n_town: Lone Keem had one bridge, one diner, and four thousand people who all knew your business. I thought it would always be there.
n_hints: The radio said Portland. Then it said Bangor. Grown ups have a way of turning off a radio that tells a child everything.
n_goodbye: The hospital called my mother in early. She hugged me at the door longer than usual. I pretended I did not notice. I wish I had held on.
n_evening: By evening the sirens had stopped sounding far away. Mister Abernathy was standing in his yard, facing the wall. He did not answer when I called his name.
n_night: At two in the morning, I heard glass break downstairs. That was the end of the quiet. And the beginning of the other kind.
n_street: The town I knew was gone in a single night. The fog was full of people who were not people anymore. They did not speak. That is why we called it the Quiet.
n_garage: There are moments that split your life in two. Before, and after. This is mine.
n_bridge: My father said, get your sister across. I will be right behind you.
n_end: He was right behind us. That is what I told myself, for a long, long time. Chapter two. High Water.
